1:
The opening question is read as a complaint about delay rather than a doubt about knowledge. Henry grants the premise in three parts, that past times are not hidden from God's judgment, present times from his providence, nor future times from his prescience, and draws the consequence that if wicked men die unpunished we cannot say they escaped him by surprise, since he foresaw it and even ordered it; Job asserts the omniscience first, he notes, as other prophets in like straits asserted the righteousness or the holiness or the goodness of God, because general truths must be held fast even where particular events cannot be reconciled to them. Ellicott reads the verse as a general perplexity rather than a private one, arising from a survey of God's dealings with the world, and observes that the second negative is so placed in our version as to make the line ambiguous, which would be cured by reading see not instead of not see. Clarke prefers an emendation that turns the question into a wish, that the Almighty would keep set days of doom, as courts keep term times, so that an accused man might look forward to one.

The catalogue of wrongs then begins with the land. Gill explains the landmarks as the stones anciently set to distinguish one man's ground from another, removed either secretly by night or openly by men with power enough to pretend they were wrongly placed, and notes that the heathen too had a Jupiter of boundaries whose stones a remover was slain for touching. Clarke gives the same practice its motive, that the posts were shifted onto a neighbour's ground so that by contracting his boundaries a man might enlarge his own, and reports two other readings of the next clause, one making the verb destroy rather than feed and one in which the Greek had read shepherd, so that both are carried off together. Henry sets the whole under the head of tyranny, wrong done under pretence of law and authority, with the tears of the oppressed unregarded and power on the side of the oppressors, and adds that forging or destroying deeds is now the crime equivalent to moving a landmark.

The poor who are robbed are then named one by one. Gill takes the ass of the fatherless as the single beast of a man who had no friend to provide for him, which made the taking of it the more inhuman, and reads the turning of the needy out of the way either of their livelihood, by the taking of what they lived by, or literally out of the road, pushed aside by a haughty man or avoiding him for fear. Wesley keeps the last of those, that they labour to keep out of the path where these oppressors walk and hide themselves for fear of further injury, and glosses the pledge taken as against the law written first in men's hearts and afterwards in Scripture. Ellicott observes that the ass and the ox are named singly because the fatherless and the widow had no more than one, that the oppression described is first of the country and then of the city, and that behind it we seem to catch a glimpse of some abject and servile race haunting the desert and suffering at the hands of stronger tribes. Clarke turns the closed path into a case from his own country, where a nobleman shut up an ancient footway and a cobbler took him to law and won it, answering those who wondered at his boldness that he did not like to leave the world worse than he found it. Keil and Delitzsch supply their own rendering of the four verses, the landmarks removed, the flocks stolen and pastured, the orphan's ass carried off and the widow's ox distrained, and the poor of the land obliged to slink away together.
5:
Who the wild asses are, and whose corn is reaped, divides the reading of the whole passage. Gill allows the comparison to be dropped and the words taken literally of the beasts whose proper place is the wilderness, though he follows the Targum in supplying the note of similitude. Wesley makes the asses a figure for the oppressors themselves, lawless and fierce and greedy of prey, who go out to spoil and rob. Clarke reads the verse of a predatory life, men who roam the wilderness and seize whatever they find, and so support themselves and their families. On the corn, Gill holds that the wicked reap the standing corn of the poor so impudently that they do not trouble to steal it from the barn, while Ellicott takes the opposite view, that the poor reap the tyrant's corn and cut his provender and go without themselves, and Wesley a third, that these robbers plundered promiscuously, even their own brethren in iniquity. Clarke keeps to the roaming hordes, who carry off grain and olives and vines in a sudden irruption and plunge with the spoil into the desert where none can follow.

The exposure of the poor is reported almost without disagreement. Gill explains that those called naked are not wholly so but thinly clad, and that even their bed clothes are taken, so that they must lie all night with nothing over them; and that lying at the foot of a hill, where the clouds gather and break or the snow melts in the heat of the day, they are drenched by the streams that run down. Clarke defends the mountain showers against an emendation that would make them torrents, having seen in mountainous country the tail of a water-spout break and pour out what would be incredible to anyone who had not watched it, and he reads the whole description as characteristic of a wandering people, ill fed, ill clothed and often without even tents, who can carry no household stuff because they may have to fly for their lives. Keil and Delitzsch supply the verses in their own rendering, the fatherless torn from the breast, the poor defrauded, the naked slinking away without clothes and bearing the sheaves while hungry, and the oil squeezed out between the walls.

The oppression of the labourers and of the city closes the section. Gill reads the plucking of the fatherless either as a design to starve the child, or to sell it into slavery, or to force the mother to wean it early so that she could be put to work. Clarke takes it of children seized to be brought up in slavery, and makes the pledge the exaction of an oppressive landlord who lets his ground at an exorbitant rent and then takes the labourer's cow or cart or bed when he cannot pay it. Henry presses the same charge against employers, that they not only give no wages, though the labourer is worthy of his hire, but will not so much as give meat and drink, so that those who carry the sheaves are hungry and those who tread the winepresses suffer thirst, which he calls worse than muzzling the ox that treads out the corn; such masters, he adds, forget that they have a Master in heaven. Ellicott marks the turn at the last verse, that here the survey moves inside the city walls, and takes the closing clause of those who caused the wrongs rather than those who suffered them. Wesley reads the cry as the blood of men wounded to death calling aloud to God for vengeance, and Clarke, who had himself been appointed to survey a poor district of a great city, found every dwelling full of people and the poor not only badly fed and clothed but wretchedly lodged.
13:
The light rebelled against is read both ways. Henry sets the figurative and the literal side by side without choosing: either they sin against the light of nature and of conscience, professing to know God while refusing to be governed by the knowledge, or they have the daylight and choose the night as the better season for wickedness. He makes the class the worst of sinners on two grounds, that they sin wilfully against their own convictions and so add rebellion to the sin, and that they sin deliberately, with plot and contrivance and a thousand arts of concealment, forgetting that there is no darkness in which a worker of iniquity can hide from God. Ellicott calls the phrase a very remarkable one which seems to anticipate the teaching of the fourth Gospel, and Wesley takes the light as reason and conscience together with the revelation then in good measure imparted, adding that not knowing its ways means not approving or choosing them.

Three trades of darkness are then named in order. Gill has the murderer rise before sunrise, when the early traveller is on the road and the labourer going out, and lie in wait in a cave or thicket for them. Clarke makes him a highwayman driven to the work by poverty and distress, who robs by daylight and murders for fear of being taken, so adding crime to crime, and turns housebreaker by night. Henry notices how small the plunder is, a little money or goods carried to market, so that the murderer ventures his own life for what hardly keeps the victim alive, and thirsts more for blood than for booty; and he turns the industry of such men into a reproach to the slothful, that the sight should shame us out of our negligence in doing good. On the adulterer Gill explains that the twilight waited for is of the evening and not the morning, since the whole night is wanted. Clarke has him mark the house, wait impatiently for the dusk, go out muffled, and then find the dawn terrible as the shadow of death lest he be recognised before he reaches his own door. Henry reads the concealment as shame and fear together, since even the most impudent of such sinners do what they can to hide the thing.

The housebreaking and the closing verse are mostly a matter of rendering. Gill reports that some take the digging through houses of the adulterers just named, but thinks such steps neither safe nor necessary, since admittance is got more easily by bribing a servant, and refers the verse to burglars proper. Ellicott offers the alternative reading of the second clause, that they shut themselves up by day rather than mark the houses beforehand, and notes the custom still reported in eastern cities of gaining access to the women's quarters in female dress; he also observes that the order of the three crimes, murder and adultery and theft, agrees with the order of the Decalogue, which at least suggests acquaintance with it. Clarke supplies the practice from his own time and place, thieves who dig through a mud wall and under a clay floor and plunder a house while the family sleeps. Gill takes the last verse to mean that the morning is alike hateful to all of them, murderer and robber and adulterer and housebreaker together, what is pleasant to other men being to these the shadow of death, since they love darkness rather than light; Wesley gives the same sense in two words, that the morning is terrible and hateful to them. Keil and Delitzsch render the whole series plainly, the murderer rising at dawn, the adulterer watching for the twilight and veiling his face, the walls dug through in the dark while they shut themselves up by day, and the depth of night serving them for morning.
18:
The swiftness upon the waters is read three ways. Gill takes the verse of yet another class of wicked men, pirates who rob upon the high seas, choosing the fastest vessels so as to run from place to place for prey and to carry off their booty when pursued, and who prefer that life to any husbandry on land. Henry gives the same reading, with privateers cruising from channel to channel for prizes, and quotes a bishop of his own church for the gloss that such men despise the employment of those who till the ground and plant vineyards as poor and unprofitable; but he offers an alternative, that the words continue the account of those who fear the light, who make off quickly when discovered and lurk, not in the vineyards where they might be seen, but in some cursed portion, a lonely place nobody looks after. Ellicott argues for that second reading and against the comparison our version makes, holding that each of these rebels against the light is swift to escape over the face of the waters, that the cursed portion means a place men regard as of evil name, and that the man turns away from the frequented road through the vineyards and chooses lone and rugged paths instead. Wesley reads it of the man rather than his flight, that he passes quickly away with all his glory, like waters that never stay in one place, and will never again see or enjoy the vineyards he leaves behind. Clarke renders the first clause literally, that light is he upon the face of the waters, and reports an emendation which makes it miserable rather than light.

The snow water is explained from the country and from the argument. Clarke fills in the picture, the public tanks which had been filled by the snow melting on the mountains and kept for irrigating the land, and which the long drought had emptied, so that relief was cut off from that quarter as from every other; he adds that the second clause is only two words in the original, and that another reading makes them say that they fall to their lowest depth. Ellicott sets the verse against Job's earlier speeches, where he had already spoken of a sudden death for the wicked as a blessing compared with the lingering torture he was himself undergoing. Keil and Delitzsch give their own rendering of the lines, drought and heat snatching away the snow water as the grave snatches away those who have sinned, and the womb forgetting the man while worms feast on him.

The last verse turns on one word and one mood. Gill offers three senses of the womb that forgets, the mother or wife or friend, any of whom may bury him in oblivion either because his life was infamous or because his death was easy; or the womb of the earth in which he lies forgotten; or God himself, since the word carries the sense of mercy. Clarke takes that last sense and presses it hard, that the word signifies compassion, so the line reads that mercy shall be unmindful of him, and he exclaims at the dreadfulness of a state in which mercy itself forgets a sinner and his perdition does not slumber; he also quotes the Chaldee, which turns the clause about the worms into a sentence on the cruel who neglected to commiserate the poor. Ellicott reports a different construction altogether, that some read the whole verse as what ought rather to be the doom of the wicked, so that it becomes a wish, his own mother forgetting him and unrighteousness being broken as a tree. Wesley keeps the plain statement and makes the breaking final, since a tree once broken down never grows again.
21:
The treatment of the barren woman is read in opposite senses. Gill takes the verb as it stands and offers several applications, a man who upbraids a barren wife and is churlish to her on that account. Wesley keeps the same sense and gives the reason it stings, that barrenness was counted a curse and a reproach, so that the man added affliction to the afflicted. Henry agrees and compares the upbraiding of Hannah by her rival, done on purpose to make her fret, and observes that the childless, like the fatherless, are in some degree helpless, which is what exposes them. Clarke reverses the line: the original should be rendered he feedeth, as the Latin took it, so that the charge is not cruelty to the barren woman but a selective kindness, the man having provided for her while leaving the widow uncomforted, being an enemy to the procreation of children and showing no mercy to large families.

Who draws the mighty, and who gives the safety, is the chapter's hardest knot. Gill makes the oppressor the subject, attacking men nearly as powerful as himself and drawing them by force or policy into his own acts of violence. Ellicott keeps the tyrant as subject but makes the drawing moral, a great man pulling others after him by influence and example so completely that no one under his sway is sure of his life. Clarke follows another commentator into a third reading, that the man draws guards about him for his defence and then, in the midst of them, does not feel assured of his life, which he calls an admirable delineation of the inquietudes of a tyrant; and he carries that reading into the next verse, where the guards are given him for security and he leans on them while his eyes are on their ways, watching his own protectors lest they plot against him. Ellicott offers a different construction of the same verse, that each of his victims pays him tribute to be left secure while the tyrant's eye is on all their ways, but grants that making God the subject, who gives the wicked man his security, makes very good sense too. Gill takes that second way outright, that it is God who gives the wicked man to be in safety, so that he is preserved from the depredations of others and dwells secure; and Wesley puts the same thing with the warning attached, that God gives them these strange successes and yet observes them all and will punish in due time.

The end of such men, and the end of the speech, close the chapter. Clarke says the same of tyrants in particular, that God puts down one and raises up another, and adds a historical observation, that few tyrants reach the eternal world by a dry death rather than a violent one, and that all eastern history is full of it. Keil and Delitzsch render the closing lines plainly, the safety given and the eyes upon their ways, the exaltation for a little while, and the challenge that follows. Ellicott reads that challenge as a claim about evidence, that Job has facts of his own as ready and as incontrovertible as those of his friends, and yet irreconcilable with theirs. Clarke makes the same point at length, that Job has proved by examples that the righteous are often oppressed and the wicked often triumph, and defies his friends to find a flaw in the argument; and he adds the comment on the whole debate that neither side could hit on the middle way, which is that the wicked man may be in prosperity and yet miserable in his soul, and the righteous man in adversity and yet happy in his God, in which respects the ways of God are always equal.
